stages.title: Mechanism analysis
stages.hook: An engine's piston slides in a straight line while the crank spins. How many independent movements does this linkage allow, and how do we know it will not jam?
explain: A mechanism is a set of rigid links joined so that motion is constrained. The number of independent inputs needed to fix its position is the degrees of freedom (DOF). For a planar mechanism the Grübler (Kutzbach) equation gives F = 3(n − 1) − 2 j₁ − j₂, where n is the number of links (including the fixed frame), j₁ the number of one-DOF joints (revolute or sliding) and j₂ the number of two-DOF joints.

A four-bar linkage has n = 4 and four revolute joints: F = 3 × 3 − 2 × 4 = 1. A slider-crank also has n = 4 and four one-DOF joints, so F = 1. One input, such as a crank angle, determines every other position. If F came out as 0 the mechanism would be locked, and if more than the number of drivers the mechanism is under-constrained.

Grashof's rule tells whether a four-bar linkage has a link that can rotate fully: if the shortest plus the longest link is no more than the sum of the other two (s + l ≤ p + q), at least one link can make a full turn. Links of 20, 50, 40 and 45 cm give 20 + 50 = 70 ≤ 40 + 45 = 85, so it is a Grashof linkage.

In a slider-crank with crank radius r turning at angular speed ω, the crank pin moves at v = ω r and the stroke of the slider is 2r (when the connecting rod is long enough). Design checks include transmission angle (the angle between coupler and follower should stay near 90°), dead-centre positions where force cannot start motion, and clearances that wear and cause backlash.

stages.title: Mechanical vibrations
stages.hook: A washing machine shakes gently at one speed, violently at another and calmly at a third. Why does the spin speed matter so much?
explain: A simple vibrating system has a mass m on a spring of stiffness k. Without damping it oscillates at the natural frequency ωₙ = √(k ÷ m) in rad/s, so f = ωₙ ÷ 2π in hertz. A 10 kg mass on a 4000 N/m spring has ωₙ = √400 = 20 rad/s and f = 3.18 Hz. The static deflection under weight is δ = m g ÷ k = 10 × 9.8 ÷ 4000 = 0.0245 m.

Damping removes vibration energy as heat. The damping ratio ζ compares actual damping with the amount that just prevents oscillation. Vehicle suspensions use ζ of about 0.2 to 0.4 as a compromise between comfort and handling.

If a force repeats at a frequency close to ωₙ, resonance occurs and the amplitude can become very large, limited only by damping. Rotating machines with an unbalance force have a forcing frequency equal to their rotation speed, so a critical speed exists where the machine speed matches a natural frequency.

Control options: avoid running at the critical speed, change k or m to move ωₙ, balance rotating parts, add damping, or isolate the machine with springs. Isolation works when the forcing frequency is above √2 times ωₙ. Failure causes include fatigue cracks from long exposure to vibration, loosened bolts and noise.

stages.title: Machine elements and transmission systems
stages.hook: A motor runs at 1200 rpm but a conveyor must move at 400 rpm with more torque. What chain of parts could do the job, and what is lost on the way?
explain: Transmission systems move power from a source to a load, changing speed, torque or direction. Belts, chains, gears and shafts are the main elements. In any ideal transmission P = T ω is conserved, so reducing speed by a ratio raises torque by the same ratio. Real drives lose some power as heat, so the output torque is multiplied by the efficiency.

Belt drives: speed ratio = D₂ ÷ D₁. A 100 mm driver and a 300 mm driven pulley give a ratio of 3, so 1200 rpm becomes 400 rpm. Belts slip and are quiet, cheap and protect from overload. Chains do not slip, so they are used where timing matters. Gears give compact, positive drives. Gear trains multiply ratios: stages of 3 and 4 give 12 overall, and with 90% total efficiency 5 N m input becomes 5 × 12 × 0.9 = 54 N m.

Bearings carry shaft loads. The basic rating life of a ball bearing is L₁₀ = (C ÷ P)³ million revolutions, where C is the dynamic load rating and P the equivalent load. With C = 20 kN and P = 10 kN, L₁₀ = 2³ = 8 million revolutions. Halving the load multiplies the life by eight.

Design checks include power rating, alignment, lubrication, guards and heat. Misalignment, over-tension, contamination and lubrication failure are leading causes of early failure. A worm gear can be self-locking, which holds loads in hoists, but it has lower efficiency.

stages.title: Turbomachinery
stages.hook: A pump's speed is doubled. Does the flow double, or does something else change much more? Be careful about the power needed.
explain: Turbomachines exchange energy between a rotating blade row and a fluid. Pumps, fans and compressors add energy to the fluid; turbines extract it. The Euler turbomachine equation links the torque on the rotor to the change in the fluid's angular momentum, so the shape of the blades and the rotor speed control the energy transfer.

The useful hydraulic power of a pump is P = ρ g Q H, with flow Q in m³/s and head H in metres. For water with Q = 0.05 m³/s and H = 20 m, P = 1000 × 9.8 × 0.05 × 20 = 9800 W. If the shaft power is 14 kW, the efficiency is 9.8 ÷ 14 = 70%.

Affinity laws predict how a pump behaves when speed N changes: Q ∝ N, H ∝ N² and shaft power ∝ N³. Doubling speed doubles the flow, makes the head four times as large and needs eight times the power. A small speed reduction therefore saves much power, which is why variable-speed drives are common.

Centrifugal pumps can suffer cavitation. If the pressure at the inlet falls below the liquid's vapour pressure, vapour bubbles form and then collapse violently, causing noise, vibration and erosion of the impeller. The net positive suction head (NPSH) available must exceed the pump's NPSH required. Running a pump with a closed discharge valve overheats the fluid, so pumps need protection.

stages.title: Hydraulic and pneumatic systems
stages.hook: An excavator arm lifts tonnes of earth through a thin hose of oil, while a dentist's drill runs on air. Why do designers choose oil for one job and air for another?
explain: Fluid power systems use a pressurised fluid to transmit force. Hydraulic systems use oil, which is almost incompressible, so they give stiff, precise motion and very high force. Pneumatic systems use compressed air, which is clean, fast and cheap but springy, so they are used for lighter, quicker tasks.

A cylinder produces force F = p A. With oil at 10 MPa on a 50 mm bore (A = π × 0.025² = 1.963 × 10⁻³ m²) the force is 19.6 kN. A pneumatic cylinder of 40 mm bore at 0.6 MPa gauge pressure gives only 754 N. Speed is set by flow: v = Q ÷ A. A flow of 0.0002 m³/s into the 50 mm cylinder moves it at 0.102 m/s. Fluid power is P = p Q = 10 × 10⁶ × 0.0002 = 2000 W.

Components: a pump or compressor makes the flow, valves direct and limit it, actuators (cylinders and motors) do the work, and accumulators store energy. A pressure relief valve opens at a set pressure to protect the system. Without it, a blocked line would let pressure rise until a hose or cylinder burst.

Safety is central. Stored pressure can move a load when a line is opened, and a pinhole leak in a high-pressure hose can inject oil into skin. Before maintenance, systems must be depressurised and loads supported mechanically. Heat, contamination and air in the oil are leading causes of failure.

Higher than the extend force, because the rod adds area
Equal, since the pressure is the same on both sides
Zero, because the rod blocks the oil

panel.q: The relief valve is set at 14 MPa but the hose is only rated at 10 MPa. What is wrong?
o: The hose may burst before the valve opens
Nothing, valves never fail so the hose is safe
The valve should be set even higher than 14 MPa
The hose is too long for the pump

A larger pump that pushes more oil
Warmer oil that flows more easily
Weaker seals that let the oil move

teach.topic: How a hydraulic cylinder produces force
teach.model: A pump pushes oil into a cylinder, and the oil pressure acts on the piston. The force equals the pressure times the piston area. Oil at 10 MPa on a piston of 0.002 m² gives 20 kN. The piston speed depends on how fast oil flows in.

stages.title: Welding and joining
stages.hook: Two steel plates can be joined by bolts, glue, solder or by melting them together. What makes a welded joint strong, and what can silently ruin it?
explain: Joining methods can be mechanical (bolts, rivets), adhesive (glue), or metallurgical (welding, brazing, soldering). Welding melts the edges of the parts, often with filler metal, so they fuse as one. Arc welding uses an electric arc; MIG/MAG feeds a wire electrode with shielding gas; TIG uses a non-consumable tungsten electrode; resistance spot welding joins sheets with current and pressure.

Brazing uses a filler that melts above 450 °C but below the parent metals; soldering uses a filler melting below 450 °C. Neither melts the parent metal. Both rely on a clean surface and on flux or protective atmosphere.

Arc heat input is HI = (V × I × 60) ÷ (1000 × v) kJ/mm when travel speed v is in mm/min. For V = 24 V, I = 200 A and v = 300 mm/min, HI = 0.96 kJ/mm; with a process efficiency of 0.8 the heat reaching the work is about 0.77 kJ/mm. Too much heat widens the heat-affected zone (HAZ) and can weaken it, while too little causes lack of fusion. Fillet-weld strength uses the throat: shear stress τ = F ÷ (0.707 × h × L), where h is the leg size and L the length.

Defects include porosity (gas holes), cracks, undercut and incomplete fusion. Preheating, clean joints, correct shielding and qualified procedures help avoid them. Safety: arcs give intense ultraviolet light, so welders need helmets with filters, fume extraction and fire precautions. Inspection by visual, dye penetrant, magnetic particle, ultrasonic or X-ray methods checks quality.

example.q: A fillet weld has a leg size of 6 mm and a length of 100 mm. It carries a shear load of 40 kN. Find the shear stress in the throat.

analogies.home: Soldering a wire joins it with a lower-melting metal, like gluing with a metal.
analogies.city: Pipelines are welded in sections, then tested by X-ray.
analogies.farm: A farmer repairs a cracked plough share by arc welding.
analogies.sea: Ship hulls are made of welded steel plates that must be leak-tight.

Metal added to fill a joint.
Joining with a filler that melts above 450 °C without melting the parent metal.

misc.wrong: A weld that looks smooth must be strong.
misc.right: Internal defects such as lack of fusion or cracks may be invisible, so inspection and qualified procedures are needed.

stages.limits: The throat formula is a simplified design check, and real welds have residual stress and distortion from uneven cooling.

trip.prompt: Find the main arc welding processes. Which one uses a shielding gas?

o: Welding melts the parent metal; brazing does not
Brazing melts the parent metal but welding does not
Welding uses no heat, only pressure and glue
They are identical processes with different names
questions.why: Brazing uses a lower-melting filler and leaves the parent metal solid.

questions.q: An arc welder uses 24 V and 200 A with a travel speed of 300 mm/min. Using HI = V I × 60 ÷ (1000 v) with no efficiency factor, what is the heat input in kJ/mm?
A fillet weld has leg size 8 mm and length 150 mm. What is its throat area, using 0.707 × leg × length, in mm²?
The weld in the previous question (throat area 848 mm²) carries 60 kN. What is the shear stress in MPa?
Why is shielding gas used in MIG welding?
o: To protect molten metal from oxygen and nitrogen in the air
To cool the wire as it feeds through the torch
To make the arc louder so the welder hears it
To add colour to the weld so it can be seen

questions.q: A weld shows porosity. Which cause is most likely?
o: Contaminated surface or shielding gas loss
Cooling the metal too slowly after welding only
Overly clean metal that has been ground bright
Too little current only, giving a cold weld
questions.why: Gas from dirt, oil, moisture or lost shielding is trapped as the metal freezes.

questions.q: A welder works without a filtered helmet because the job is short. What is the danger?
o: Arc eye and burns from ultraviolet and intense light
None, the job is short so the risk is small
Cold hands from the metal after welding
Noise from the arc only, which is harmless to eyes
questions.why: Arc light injures the eyes and skin quickly, even in brief exposures.

questions.q: Thick steel is welded without preheat in cold weather and cracks appear beside the weld. Why?
o: Fast cooling makes the HAZ hard and brittle
Slow cooling, which softens the steel too much
Too much preheat, which makes the steel brittle
The weld is too thin to hold the plates together
questions.why: Fast cooling in the heat-affected zone can form hard brittle structures, and preheating slows the cooling.

questions.q: Compare bolting and welding for joining two structural parts, giving one advantage of each.
questions.model: Bolted joints can be taken apart for maintenance or replacement and need little skilled heat work on site. Welded joints are continuous, leak-tight and can be lighter and stronger as there are no holes or extra plates.
questions.why: Each method suits different needs for strength, sealing and servicing.

questions.q: Match each process to its description.
pairs: Sheets joined by current and pressure
questions.why: These are common joining processes.

panel.q: Aluminium is welded with the same settings as steel and the plate burns through. Why?
o: Aluminium conducts heat well and melts at a lower temperature, so settings must change
Aluminium does not conduct heat at all, so the plate stays cold and then collapses
It has a higher melting point than steel, so the arc overheats it quickly
It cannot be welded, so the plate must be cut away
panel.why: Different thermal properties need different procedures.

panel.q: A pressure vessel weld passes visual inspection. Why is radiographic or ultrasonic testing still required?
o: Internal flaws can be invisible but dangerous
Visual checks are unlawful for pressure vessels
It makes the weld shinier and stronger
It costs nothing so it is always worth doing as an extra
panel.why: Hidden defects can cause sudden failure under pressure.

panel.q: Welding near a container that held petrol, even if empty, is dangerous because of what?
o: Residual vapours can explode
The container is too cold to weld safely
Metal does not conduct heat, so it builds up
Welds are weaker next to empty petrol cans
panel.why: Vapours or residues ignite from sparks and heat. Containers must be cleaned and tested first.

teach.model: A good weld fuses the metals into one piece without holes or cracks. It needs clean surfaces, the right heat, shielding from the air and a qualified method. After welding it is inspected, because defects can be hidden inside. The welder must also wear eye and skin protection.

points.ask: What can go wrong and how do we check?
How does the welder stay safe?

stages.title: Machining and CNC fundamentals
stages.hook: A CNC lathe turns a shaft to within a few hundredths of a millimetre. How does it know how fast to spin, how far to move and when the cutter is wearing out?
explain: Machining removes material with a cutting tool. In turning, the workpiece rotates and a tool moves along it; in milling, the tool rotates and the work moves; drilling makes round holes. The key variables are cutting speed v (m/min), feed f (mm per revolution) and depth of cut d (mm).

Cutting speed relates to spindle speed N (rpm) and diameter D (mm): v = π D N ÷ 1000. For D = 50 mm and N = 800 rpm, v = 125.7 m/min. To get 100 m/min on a 40 mm bar: N = 1000 × 100 ÷ (π × 40) = 796 rpm. The time to turn a length L is t = L ÷ (f × N): for L = 120 mm, f = 0.2 mm/rev and N = 600 rpm, t = 1 minute.

CNC (computer numerical control) machines follow programmed instructions, often G-code. G00 moves rapidly, G01 moves in a straight line at the set feed, G02/G03 cut arcs, and M03 starts the spindle clockwise. Coordinates define the tool path. Tools wear, so the program includes tool offsets and the operator checks wear.

Machining faces trade-offs between speed, tool life and surface finish. Too high a speed overheats and ruins the tool. Safety is crucial: guards must be in place, swarf is sharp and hot, long hair and loose clothing and gloves near rotating parts are forbidden, and workpieces must be clamped securely before starting the spindle.

example.q: A bar of diameter 40 mm is turned at a cutting speed of 100 m/min. What spindle speed is needed?

Too much coolant only, which shocks the tool
Speed too low, which rubs the tool
Feed set to zero so the tool only rubs

o: An unclamped part can be thrown out at high speed
It saves time when cutting begins
It reduces noise only, and is not a safety matter
It cools the work so it does not expand

Increase the feed per revolution
Remove the coolant from the cut
Use a blunt tool that rubs the surface smooth

Nothing, because the machine corrects it by itself
The machine will be quieter in use
The tool will be sharper and cut better

questions.why: Crashes are prevented by verification and careful set-up.

panel.q: A deep bore rattles and leaves a wavy surface. Which cause is likely?
o: Chatter from a tool overhanging too far
Too much coolant flooding the cut
The part is too cold to be machined
The spindle is switched off while cutting

panel.q: The diameter of turned parts slowly drifts bigger over the shift. What is the most probable reason?
o: Tool wear
Perfect cutting
Cooler air
Faster speed

panel.q: Why is coolant used when machining many metals?

It adds heat to the cut and the tool
It increases friction at the tool tip
It makes chips stick to the work
panel.why: Cooling and lubrication extend tool life and improve finish.

teach.model: Cutting speed is how fast the cutting edge moves past the metal. It depends on the diameter and the spindle speed. For a 40 mm bar at 100 m/min, the spindle must turn at about 796 rpm. Too fast and the tool burns out, too slow and the job takes longer.

stages.title: Computer-aided design
stages.hook: A designer changes one dimension in a CAD model and every drawing, assembly and mass value updates itself. How is that possible?
explain: Computer-aided design (CAD) builds a digital model of a part or assembly. Parametric CAD stores a model as a sequence of features (sketches, extrudes, holes, fillets) controlled by dimensions and constraints. Changing a dimension updates every feature that depends on it, and the drawings generated from the model.

Solid models give volume, mass, centre of gravity and moments of inertia. A block of 100 × 60 × 20 mm with a 20 mm through-hole in the 20 mm direction has volume 120 000 − π × 10² × 20 = 113 717 mm³. At the density of steel (7850 kg/m³) its mass is 113 717 × 10⁻⁹ × 7850 = 0.893 kg.

Assemblies position parts using mates (coincident, concentric, distance). Interference checks find parts that overlap, and tolerance analysis estimates how variation adds up. If three parts are each 20 ± 0.1 mm, the worst-case stack is 60 ± 0.3 mm, while a statistical (root-sum-square) estimate is ± √(3 × 0.1²) = ± 0.173 mm.

Design decisions: model with intent (use constraints that reflect how the part should change), add fillets where stress would concentrate, and design for manufacture. Neutral formats such as STEP exchange geometry between systems. A model is a representation; it must be checked, for example by prototype tests, because errors in units, constraints or assumptions can cause real failures.

example.q: Compute the mass of a steel block 100 × 60 × 20 mm with a 20 mm diameter hole through the 20 mm thickness. Use density 7850 kg/m³ and π = 3.1416.
steps: Hole volume = π × 10² × 20 = 6283 mm³, so net volume = 113 717 mm³.

analogies.home: A spreadsheet recalculates all results when you change one number, like a parametric model.
analogies.city: Architects use building models to check clashes between pipes and beams.
analogies.farm: A farm machine designer tests a digital hitch before cutting steel.
analogies.tech: A game character is built from linked parts and changes shape when one part moves.

A rule such as parallel or equal that controls geometry.
An assembly relation that positions one part relative to another.
A neutral file format for exchanging 3D geometry.

misc.wrong: If the CAD model looks right, the part will work.
misc.right: CAD shows geometry, not strength or manufacturability. Analysis and tests are still needed, and a poorly constrained model can break when edited.

The colour of the parts in the assembly
The price of each part supplied
The weight of the whole assembly only

The hole is too round for the software
The file is too small to be edited
CAD software never rebuilds a model
questions.why: Broken references or over-constraint cause rebuild errors, so good modelling intent matters.

o: It is unlikely that all parts are at their limits in the same direction
Statistics always lower tolerances on every drawing
Parts shrink slightly when they are put together
The calculation ignores the sizes of the parts completely
questions.why: Random variations partly cancel, but it assumes the process is controlled.

questions.q: A design is sent to a supplier in a neutral file format. What risk remains?
o: Feature history and some data may be lost
The part gets heavier when it is exported
The format is illegal to send to a supplier
Nothing at all, since every detail is kept

questions.q: Why do designers often add a fillet to an inside corner of a part in CAD?
questions.model: A sharp inside corner concentrates stress and can start cracks, especially under repeated loads. A fillet spreads the stress, and a rounded corner is easier for a cutter or mould to produce.
questions.why: Fillets reduce stress concentration and help manufacture.

pairs: Turns a profile into a solid
questions.why: These are the building blocks of CAD work.

panel.q: A designer enters a 20 mm dimension in inches mode by mistake. What is the danger?
o: The part is made far too big
The part is smaller by a hundred times
The file is deleted
Nothing
panel.why: 20 inches is 508 mm. Unit settings must be checked.

panel.q: Why run a simulation on a CAD model before building a prototype?
o: To find overstress or interference early and cheaply
To avoid all physical testing later in the project
To remove the need for any materials
To make the part lighter automatically without changes
panel.why: Virtual testing is cheaper but still must be validated.

panel.q: A part needs a hole to be exactly central after any width change. Which CAD approach helps?
o: Constrain the hole symmetric to the width edges
Type the number as a fixed value
Draw the hole by eye in the right place
Delete the hole and cut it by hand later
panel.why: A constraint captures design intent, so the hole stays centred as the width changes.

teach.model: A parametric model remembers how it was built and what dimensions control it. If you change one dimension, all the linked features, drawings and mass values update. This saves time and cuts errors, but only if the model was built with good constraints and the designer still checks the result.

stages.title: Manufacturing quality control
stages.hook: A machine makes shafts of 10 mm diameter, but no two are exactly the same. How can a factory know whether the process is under control before any bad parts are made?
explain: No process makes identical parts. Variation comes from tool wear, temperature, material and operators. Quality control measures and manages that variation. Inspection tools include micrometres, calipers, gauges and coordinate measuring machines (CMMs). A measurement system must itself be checked for repeatability and reproducibility (gauge R&R).

Statistical process control (SPC) plots sample averages on a control chart. The centre line is the process mean; control limits sit at ±3σ ÷ √n. For a process with mean 50, σ = 0.6 and samples of n = 4, the upper limit is 50 + 3 × 0.6 ÷ 2 = 50.9. A point outside the limits, or a trend, signals a special cause that should be investigated.

Capability compares the spread with the specification limits. Cp = (USL − LSL) ÷ (6σ). For limits of 10.10 and 9.90 and σ = 0.025, Cp = 0.20 ÷ 0.15 = 1.33. Cpk also considers centring: Cpk = min(USL − μ, μ − LSL) ÷ 3σ. With a mean of 10.03, Cpk = 0.07 ÷ 0.075 = 0.93, which is not capable even though Cp looks fine.

Quality is also built in by design: tolerances that match the process capability, error-proofing (poka-yoke), clear work instructions and traceability. Safety-critical parts get stricter checks. Rejecting only at the end is expensive and wasteful, so prevention is better than detection.

example.q: Specification limits are 10.10 and 9.90 mm. The process mean is 10.03 mm with σ = 0.025 mm. Find Cp and Cpk.
steps: Distance from mean to nearest limit = 10.10 − 10.03 = 0.07 mm.

analogies.city: A bus company tracks arrival times to find when delays start.
analogies.farm: Weighing sacks as they are filled shows if the scale is drifting.

stages.mnemonic: Measure, plot, watch for trends, fix the cause.
terms: A plot of process measurements over time with control limits.
Ratio of the specification width to six standard deviations.
Capability index that includes how well the process is centred.
A study of measurement repeatability and reproducibility.

misc.wrong: If every part passes inspection, the process must be good.
misc.right: A process can drift toward the limits while parts still pass. Control charts and capability studies show trends before defects occur.

trip.prompt: Find a control chart example. Which points would you investigate?

questions.q: What does a control chart signal when a point falls outside the control limits?
o: A likely special cause worth investigating
The process is perfect and needs no further attention
The measurement unit is always wrong when this happens
The operator must be replaced at once
questions.why: Out-of-limit points are unlikely from normal variation alone.

questions.q: A process has a mean of 50, σ = 0.6 and samples of n = 4. What is the upper control limit for the sample mean (mean + 3σ ÷ √n)?
Specification limits are 20.20 mm and 19.80 mm and σ = 0.05 mm. What is Cp?
Specification limits 10.10 and 9.90 mm, mean 10.03 mm, σ = 0.025 mm. What is Cpk to two decimals?
Cp is 1.4 but Cpk is 0.8. What does that suggest?
o: The spread is fine but the process is off-centre
The spread is too large for the limits
The measurement system is perfect
The limits on the drawing are wrong
questions.why: Cpk lower than Cp means the mean is shifted toward one limit.

questions.q: A seven-point run of values all rising, inside the limits, appears on a control chart. What should be done?
o: Investigate for tool wear or drift
Nothing, they are inside the limits
Stop the chart
Widen the limits
questions.why: Trends show a non-random cause even before limits are crossed.

questions.q: A gauge gives different readings when two operators measure the same part. Which study reveals this?
o: Gauge R&R
Cp
Hardness test
Tensile test
questions.why: Reproducibility is the variation between operators.

questions.q: Why is error-proofing (poka-yoke) better than inspecting at the end?
o: It prevents the defect from being made
It makes the final inspection take longer
It hides defects until the customer finds them
It increases waste in the factory
questions.why: Prevention is cheaper and safer than detection.

questions.q: Explain why a factory might reduce the tolerance on a critical part only after confirming its process capability.
questions.model: If the process spread is larger than the tolerance, a tighter tolerance will lead to many rejected parts and high cost. Capability studies show whether the process can hold the tolerance consistently.
questions.why: Tolerances must match what the process can actually produce.

questions.q: Match each tool to what it does.
questions.why: Different tools suit different checks.

panel.q: A process with Cpk = 1.0 makes about how many defects per million (centred, normal)?
o: About 2700
About 63
About 0.002
About 317 000
panel.why: Cpk = 1 corresponds to limits at 3σ, giving about 0.27% outside, which is 2700 per million.

panel.q: An airline part is tested by taking a sample of 5 from each batch of 10 000. A flaw affects 1 in 1000 parts. What is the risk?
o: The sample may miss the flaw, so critical parts need 100% inspection or process control
Sampling always finds every flaw, so no more checks are needed
The flaw does not matter because only 1 in 1000 parts has it
Batches should be cut to a single part each
panel.why: Small samples can miss rare defects. Safety-critical items need stronger controls.

panel.q: A supervisor suggests changing the machine setting every time a part is slightly off the target. What does this tend to do?
o: Increase the variation (over-adjustment)
Reduce the variation to zero over time
Improve the capability of the process
Make the control chart perfectly flat
panel.why: Reacting to common-cause noise adds variation, so adjust only when the chart signals a special cause.

teach.topic: What a control chart tells a factory
teach.model: A control chart plots measurements of a process over time with limits around the average. If a point lies outside the limits, or the points show a steady trend, something has changed, like a worn tool. The factory can fix it before many bad parts are made.

points.ask: What do you put on the chart?
